23474: The Bible insists there is only one God, yet it speaks of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each as God. Christians summed this up as the Trinity: one God in three persons. It is not three gods, and it is not one person wearing three masks.
23475: God is one in being and three in persons; the doctrine is a boundary around a mystery, not a maths problem.
23477: Israel's core confession is that the LORD is one, and there is no other God besides him. The New Testament keeps this confession rather than abandoning it.
23478: Father, Son and Spirit are each God
23479: The Father is called God, the Word who became flesh is called God, and lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God. The three are named together as one 'name' in baptism and blessing, and they speak to and about one another.
23480: If there is only one God, how can three distinct persons, who pray to, send and glorify one another, each be fully God? Counting seems to give either one person (and the distinctions collapse) or three gods (and monotheism collapses).
23482: Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches; Athanasius, the Cappadocian Fathers (Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa), Augustine; the Nicene Creed (325, 381) and the Athanasian Creed
23483: 'One' and 'three' answer different questions. Asked 'what is God?', the answer is one divine being or nature (Greek ousia). Asked 'who is God?', the answer is Father, Son and Spirit, three persons (hypostases) distinguished only by their relations: the Father begets, the Son is begotten, the Spirit proceeds. So there is no contradiction, because God is not one and three in the same respect.
23486: Some modern theologians, e.g. Jürgen Moltmann, Richard Swinburne, Cornelius Plantinga Jr.; drawing on Eastern emphasis on the persons
23487: Starts from the three persons as distinct centres of love and will, united in such perfect mutual indwelling (perichoresis) that they are one God. The unity is like a perfect family or community, only far deeper. Critics, including many classical theologians, warn this drifts toward three gods; defenders reply that the indwelling is stronger than any human union.
23490: Augustine (*On the Trinity*), Thomas Aquinas; much of the Western tradition
23491: Starts from the one God and uses analogies from a single mind: the mind, its self-knowledge and its self-love are one mind yet genuinely distinct. The Son is like God's perfect Word or self-knowledge and the Spirit like God's love. Critics say this risks making the persons mere aspects; defenders insist the analogy is only a pointer and that the persons are real.
23494: Oneness Pentecostals (one God revealed in three modes, a form of modalism); Unitarians and Jehovah's Witnesses (only the Father is fully God)
23495: These traditions remove the tension by giving up one pole. Oneness teaching keeps full deity but denies three distinct persons, reading Father, Son and Spirit as titles or manifestations of the one Jesus. Unitarian views keep the distinct persons but deny that the Son and Spirit are fully God. Trinitarians answer that Jesus prays to the Father and the Father speaks from heaven at the baptism (against modalism), and that worship and divine titles given to Jesus (against Unitarianism) require both poles.
23496: One cannot equal three. The doctrine is a self-contradiction that the church invented in the fourth century to paper over conflicting texts.
23497: A contradiction requires saying God is one and three in the same sense at the same time. The creeds say one in being and three in persons, which is not formally contradictory, even if it is beyond full understanding. Historically, the creeds did not invent the raw data: earliest Christian worship already prayed to Jesus and baptized in the threefold name. What the fourth century did was choose words to guard both sets of texts at once.
23498: Christians pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, so the doctrine shapes ordinary prayer. Many also see in it that love and relationship are not add-ons to God but part of who God is, which grounds the claim that 'God is love' even before creation existed.
23499: God does not change, yet God relents
23500: Some verses say God never changes and does not repent like a human. Others say the LORD relented, or regretted, or changed course after people prayed or repented. Both sets of texts sit side by side, sometimes in the same chapter.
23501: Scripture holds that God's character and purposes are fixed, while his dealings with people genuinely respond to them.
23502: God does not change his mind
23503: God is not a man that he should lie or repent. The LORD does not change, and the Glory of Israel will not lie or relent.
23505: After Moses intercedes, the LORD relents of the disaster he had threatened. God regrets making Saul king. He relents over Nineveh when it repents, and describes himself as one who turns from threatened judgement.
23506: 1 Samuel 15 says in verse 11 that God regretted making Saul king and in verse 29 that God does not regret. If God truly changes course, is he unchanging? If he never changes, are the 'relenting' passages misleading?
23508: A broad consensus of commentators across Jewish and Christian traditions; reflected in Jeremiah 18 itself
23509: Jeremiah 18 gives the rule: when God announces disaster on a nation and it turns, he relents; when he promises good and it turns to evil, he withholds it. The threats were conditional all along. What never changes is God's character, always against evil and always merciful to the repentant. Because God is unchanging in that sense, his response to people changes when they change.
23511: Many Church Fathers, Thomas Aquinas, John Calvin, classical theism generally
23512: God's being and will do not change in time. Scripture describes him 'as if' he repents because that is how his action looks from our side, much as we say the sun rises. The language is real communication pitched to human understanding, but it describes the effect on us rather than an emotional shift in God. 1 Samuel 15:29 is the plain teaching that controls how verse 11 is read.
23514: Open theists such as Clark Pinnock, John Sanders, Gregory Boyd; some relational and process-leaning theologians
23515: God's character is unchanging, but he genuinely interacts in time, genuinely responds to prayer and sometimes genuinely changes his plans. The 'does not repent' texts mean God does not lie or break his word, not that he never responds. Critics say this makes God dependent on creatures and undercuts his foreknowledge; defenders say it takes the narrative texts at face value.
23517: Many Old Testament scholars (e.g. Terence Fretheim, Walter Brueggemann) and some Jewish interpreters
23518: The point of 1 Samuel 15 is that God really grieved over Saul, but, unlike a fickle human, he will not be talked out of the judgement now decided. The same God who invites intercession, as with Moses, also has moments where the decision is final. Both kinds of texts are true descriptions of a personal God in covenant relationship.
23519: The same chapter says God regretted and that God never regrets. That is a flat contradiction left in by careless editors.
23520: The two statements are a few verses apart in one carefully told story, so the narrator surely saw them. The most natural reading is that they mean different things: verse 11 describes grief over what Saul became, verse 29 says God will not reverse the verdict now spoken. Readers may weigh the explanations differently, but the text itself signals that it is making a deliberate point.
23521: This paradox is why intercessory prayer makes sense in scripture. Moses, Amos and the people of Nineveh act as if their response matters to God, and the texts say it did, while believers can also rest in a God whose goodness and promises do not wobble.
23526: The Bible says God works all things according to his will and directs even kings' hearts. It also calls people to choose, holds them responsible and pleads with them to turn. Christians have argued for centuries about how both can be true.
23527: Scripture affirms both God's rule over everything and real human choice and responsibility; traditions differ on how they fit together.
23529: God works all things according to the counsel of his will. He turns the king's heart, directs our steps, does what he pleases among the inhabitants of earth, and even the crucifixion happened by his set plan.
23531: God sets life and death before Israel and says 'choose life'. Joshua says 'choose this day'. Jesus laments that Jerusalem was not willing. The same men who acted by God's plan are called lawless and guilty.
23532: If God determines everything, how are human choices free and blameworthy? If humans can thwart what God wants, in what sense is God sovereign?
23534: Augustine (later works), John Calvin, Jonathan Edwards, Reformed and many Baptist theologians
23535: Freedom means acting according to your own desires without outside compulsion, and that is compatible with God ordaining all things. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant it for good in the same act. People are responsible because they do what they want; God is sovereign because he ordains what happens without being the author of sin.
23536: Libertarian freedom with foreknowledge (Arminian and Wesleyan)
23537: Jacob Arminius, John Wesley, Methodists, many Pentecostals and free-church evangelicals; most Eastern Orthodox in their own terms
23538: God sovereignly chose to create beings with real power to choose otherwise, and gives prevenient grace that enables everyone to respond. He foreknows all choices and weaves them into his purposes, but does not cause them. Sovereignty is God's freely chosen way of ruling, not micro-determination.
23540: Luis de Molina; modern defenders such as William Lane Craig and Alvin Plantinga
23541: God knows not only what will happen but what any free creature would freely do in any circumstance. By choosing which world to create, he secures his purposes exactly while creatures choose freely. Critics ask what grounds such knowledge; defenders point to texts where God knows what would have happened.
23543: Eastern Orthodox theology (synergy), many Catholic theologians, and pastors across traditions (e.g. J. I. Packer's 'antinomy')
23544: Scripture teaches both truths without explaining how they meet, and we should preach both fully rather than shave either down. Orthodoxy speaks of synergy: grace and human will cooperate, with grace always first. The aim is to hold both poles practically rather than solve the puzzle speculatively.
23545: Either God controls everything, in which case punishing people is unjust, or he does not, in which case he is not all-powerful. Christians want it both ways.
23546: Each major tradition offers a defined account that avoids formal contradiction: compatibilists redefine freedom, libertarians redefine the scope of control, Molinists add middle knowledge. One may find one or all of them unpersuasive, but the question is which account is true, not whether any coherent account exists. Philosophers outside the church debate the same problem about causation and free will.
23547: Believers pray as if everything depends on God and act as if their choices matter, because scripture models both. Pastorally, the sovereignty pole comforts in suffering, while the responsibility pole guards against fatalism and passivity.
23549: God hardens hearts, yet holds people responsible
23550: In the Exodus story the text says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart and that God hardened Pharaoh's heart. Paul later uses this to say God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills. Yet Pharaoh is still judged for his stubbornness.
23551: Hardening in scripture is both something people do to themselves and something God does, often as a judgement that confirms a path already chosen.
23553: God tells Moses in advance he will harden Pharaoh's heart, and later the text says the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart. Paul draws the conclusion that God hardens whom he wills.
23555: When the frog plague lifted, Pharaoh hardened his heart. After hail, he sinned yet more and hardened his heart. Scripture warns, 'do not harden your hearts'.
23556: If God hardened Pharaoh, how can Pharaoh be blamed? If Pharaoh hardened himself, what does it mean that God did it?
23557: Judicial hardening: God gives people over
23558: Many Fathers (e.g. Origen, John Chrysostom), Arminian and Wesleyan commentators, and many moderate Reformed scholars
23559: Notice the sequence: in the first five plagues the text says Pharaoh hardened his heart or that his heart was hard; from the sixth plague on, God hardens it. God confirms and strengthens a choice Pharaoh already made, as a judgement, much as Romans 1 says God gave people over to what they wanted. Responsibility rests on Pharaoh's prior choices.
23561: Augustine (later works), John Calvin, many Reformed exegetes (e.g. Thomas Schreiner, John Piper)
23562: God announced the hardening before the plagues began, and Paul uses it to show God's freedom in mercy and hardening. God hardens not by putting evil into a neutral heart but by withholding softening grace from a heart already sinful. Pharaoh remains responsible because he does exactly what he wants; God remains just because no one deserves mercy.
23563: Corporate and historical reading of Romans 9
23564: Many New Perspective and Arminian scholars, e.g. N. T. Wright, and some Jewish-Christian readings
23565: Paul is not talking about individual eternal destinies but about God's freedom to use nations and people, including a hardened Pharaoh and a partially hardened Israel, in his saving plan. The hardening of Israel is partial and temporary, aimed at the inclusion of the nations and Israel's eventual restoration.
23567: Many Old Testament scholars and Jewish commentators
23568: Ancient Hebrew writers often attribute results to God as the one ultimately behind everything without denying human agency. Saying both 'God hardened' and 'Pharaoh hardened' is a way of seeing one event from two levels: the human decision and God's overarching judgement in history.
23569: God forced Pharaoh to refuse and then punished Egypt for refusing. That is a rigged game.
23570: The text does not present Pharaoh as a willing man overridden; it shows a ruler already enslaving and killing Hebrew children who repeatedly breaks his word. On most readings God's hardening confirms or uses that character rather than creating it. Whether that fully answers the moral question depends on one's view of judgement, but the story is not of an innocent being forced into evil.
23571: The warning 'today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts' is the main application the New Testament draws. Each refusal of what one knows to be right makes the next refusal easier.
23573: God is love, and God is a consuming fire
23574: John writes that God is love. Hebrews and Deuteronomy say God is a consuming fire. People often feel these pull in opposite directions: is God tender or terrifying?
23575: Scripture presents God's love and holiness as one reality, not two moods in conflict.
23577: God is love, and he showed it by sending his Son. He is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, rejoicing over his people with singing.
23579: The LORD is a consuming fire and a jealous God. Who can stand when he appears? Our God is a consuming fire, so serve him with reverence and awe.
23580: If God is love, why the language of fire, wrath and judgement? If God is fire, how can his love be safe to trust?
23581: Holy love: wrath as love's opposition to evil
23582: Most mainstream Protestant and Catholic theologians, e.g. P. T. Forsyth, John Stott
23583: God's wrath is not a mood swing but his settled opposition to what destroys what he loves. A parent who did not burn with anger at what harms their child would love less, not more. Kindness and severity are two sides of one character, as Romans 11 puts it.
23584: Refining fire: the fire is love itself
23585: Eastern Orthodox theology (e.g. Isaac the Syrian, as often summarized), George MacDonald, many Christian universalists
23586: The same fire of God's presence is experienced as warmth by those who love him and as torment by those who resist him. The fire refines like a smelter's fire. On this view the fire is not opposite to love but is what love feels like to resistance.
23587: Love and justice as co-equal attributes
23588: Classical Reformed theology (e.g. Francis Turretin, Louis Berkhof)
23589: God's justice is not a function of his love but an equally essential attribute. Love explains why he saves; justice explains why sin must be punished. The cross is where both are satisfied, so neither must be shaved down.
23590: A loving being does not threaten fire. The Bible shows an angry tribal god in the Old Testament and a nicer god in the New.
23591: Both images appear in both Testaments: 'consuming fire' is quoted in Hebrews, and the self-description 'compassionate and gracious' comes from Exodus. Whatever one concludes, the biblical writers did not see two gods; they saw one God whose love is serious enough to oppose evil. The real question is whether that combination is morally coherent, and most human ethics accepts that love can include anger at harm.
23592: Believers can approach God with confidence and with reverence at once. The paradox guards against a sentimental God who does not care about evil, and against a harsh God who cannot be loved.
23593: No one can see God, yet some saw him
23594: God tells Moses that no one can see his face and live, and John says no one has ever seen God. Yet Moses, Aaron and the elders 'saw the God of Israel' and ate a meal, Jacob says he saw God face to face, and Isaiah saw the Lord on a throne.
23595: God's full essence is invisible to human eyes, yet God really makes himself seen in forms people can bear, above all in Jesus.
23597: No one can see God's face and live. No one has ever seen God. He dwells in unapproachable light.
23599: Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders saw the God of Israel and ate and drank. Jacob saw God face to face. Isaiah saw the Lord. The LORD spoke with Moses face to face.
23600: If seeing God means death and no one has seen him, what did Moses, the elders, Jacob and Isaiah see?
23601: Theophanies: God in a bearable form
23602: Most Jewish and Christian interpreters; Exodus itself, which reports only what was under God's feet
23603: What people saw were real but mediated appearances: a form, a glory, the 'back' of God, the pavement under his feet. Exodus 24 describes only what was beneath him, and Exodus 33 lets Moses see God's back but not his face. They truly saw God, but not God's unveiled essence.
23604: The Son as the visible God
23605: Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian and many later Christian writers
23606: John 1:18 says no one has seen God, but the only Son has made him known. Many early Christians held that Old Testament appearances, such as the Angel of the LORD, were the pre-incarnate Son. The invisible Father is seen in the Son, so Jesus can say, 'whoever has seen me has seen the Father'.
23608: Eastern Orthodox theology, especially Gregory Palamas
23609: God's essence, what God is in himself, can never be seen or known by any creature. God's energies, his real presence and activity, can be truly experienced, including as uncreated light as at the Transfiguration. The visions are real encounters with God's energies, not his essence.
23610: Now and not yet: the beatific vision
23611: Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, Catholic and many Protestant theologians
23612: In this life people see God only in veiled ways; the face-to-face vision is a future promise to the pure in heart. Exodus 33 states what is true now, and Revelation 22 states what will be true then.
23613: The Bible flatly says no one has seen God and also that people saw God. One of them must be wrong.
23614: Exodus itself holds both: in chapter 33 Moses speaks with God 'face to face' in verse 11 and is told he cannot see God's face in verse 20. That suggests the writer uses 'see' at different levels, a familiar relationship versus seeing God's unveiled being. The tension is deliberate, not an oversight.
23615: Christians look to Jesus as the clearest view of what God is like, while keeping humility about how much any human grasps. It also frames worship as both intimate and awed.
23617: God tempts no one, yet God tested Abraham
23618: James says God tempts no one. Genesis 22 says God tested Abraham, and the King James Version even says God 'did tempt' him. The Greek and Hebrew words can mean both 'test' and 'tempt', which is part of the puzzle.
23619: God tests people to prove and strengthen faith; he never entices anyone to sin.
23621: Let no one say when tempted that God is tempting him; God cannot be tempted by evil and himself tempts no one. Each is tempted by his own desire.
23623: God tested Abraham by telling him to offer Isaac. God led Israel through the wilderness to test them. The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted. Believers pray 'lead us not into temptation'.
23624: If God tests people, including with heavy demands, how can James say he tempts no one?
23627: The same word (Hebrew nasah, Greek peirazo) covers both. A test aims to prove and strengthen, as gold is tested in fire; a temptation aims to make you fall. God tests for good; the devil and our own desires tempt toward evil. James even uses the same word for 'trials' that produce endurance in verse 2 and for 'temptation' toward sin in verse 13.
23629: Many patristic and Protestant writers; suggested by the parallel accounts in Samuel and Chronicles
23630: Where scripture attributes a testing to God, another agent often carries it out: Satan with Job, Satan in Chronicles where Samuel says God moved David. God allows the trial within limits for his good purposes, but the enticement to evil comes from elsewhere.
23632: Jewish tradition (the Akedah) and many Christian readers, e.g. Hebrews 11
23633: God never intended Isaac to die; he stopped Abraham and provided a ram. The test revealed and deepened Abraham's trust that God would provide, even raise the dead. Hebrews and James read it as faith proven by action, not a temptation to murder.
23634: Asking a father to kill his son is about as strong a temptation to evil as one can imagine. Calling it a 'test' is word games.
23635: Readers have felt this weight for millennia, and Jewish and Christian traditions do not treat it lightly. Within the story, the reader is told from the first verse that it is a test and that God stops it. In a culture that knew child sacrifice, many interpreters read the outcome as God decisively rejecting it. Whether one finds that satisfying is a fair question, but the text frames it as proving trust, not enticing to sin.
23636: When hardship comes, Christians are taught not to blame God for their sinful impulses, and also not to see trials as meaningless. The prayer 'lead us not into temptation' asks God to keep the trial from becoming a fall.
23641: The New Testament calls Jesus God and shows him receiving worship, forgiving sins and sharing God's glory. It also shows him born, hungry, tired, weeping, growing in wisdom and dying. Christians confess he is both, completely, in one person.
23642: Jesus is one person who is truly God and truly human, without either nature being diluted or mixed.
23644: The Word was God. In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily. Thomas calls him 'my Lord and my God'. He is 'our great God and Saviour'.
23646: The Word became flesh. He grew in wisdom and stature, was tired, wept, was tempted in every way as we are, and was made like his brothers in every respect.
